questions.stem: After receiving report, which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client with COPD whose oxygen saturation is 89% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula
A client 6 hours after a thyroidectomy who has new high-pitched sounds on inspiration
A client with a hip fracture who rates pain 7 out of 10
A client with type 2 diabetes whose glucose before lunch is 250 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Airway comes first: new stridor after neck surgery can progress to complete obstruction.

perOption.a: A saturation of 88% to 92% is often the target for clients with COPD.
perOption.b: Stridor signals airway obstruction from edema, hematoma or hypocalcemia-induced laryngospasm; it is an airway emergency.
perOption.c: Pain needs treatment soon but is not life-threatening.
perOption.d: Hyperglycemia needs follow-up but is not an immediate threat.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize an airway threat over other abnormal findings.

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client in sickle cell crisis who rates pain 9 out of 10 and is due for an opioid in 30 minutes
A client with suspected appendicitis who says the abdominal pain suddenly went away, now with a heart rate of 118/min
A client with a urinary tract infection whose temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F)
A client with gastroenteritis who vomited twice this morning

rationale.correct: An unexpected change, such as sudden pain relief with new tachycardia, outranks expected findings, even severe pain.

perOption.a: Severe pain is a priority, but the medication is scheduled and the client's condition is expected.
perOption.b: Sudden relief of appendicitis pain followed by tachycardia suggests perforation, which can lead to peritonitis and sepsis.
perOption.c: A low-grade fever is expected with infection and is not unstable.
perOption.d: Vomiting needs monitoring for dehydration but is not an emergency.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize perforation of the appendix as an emergency.

questions.stem: The charge nurse is reviewing updates on four clients. Which client needs the nurse's attention first?

options.text: A client 1 hour after a cardiac catheterization who needs vital signs checked
A client receiving vancomycin whose trough level is due before the next dose
A client with a chest tube who has gentle tidaling in the water seal chamber
A client with a head injury whose right pupil is now larger than the left and sluggish

rationale.correct: A change in pupil size and reaction is a late, ominous sign of increased intracranial pressure.

perOption.a: Routine post-procedure checks can be done next or delegated if the client is stable.
perOption.b: The trough level is timed with the next dose and can wait.
perOption.c: Tidaling with breathing is expected and shows the system is working.
perOption.d: A new unequal, sluggish pupil signals rising intracranial pressure and possible brain herniation.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A client 1 day after abdominal surgery has pain rated 6 out of 10, is anxious about going home, has weak, ineffective coughing with coarse crackles, and has not walked yet. Which problem is the priority?

options.text: Ineffective airway clearance
Acute pain
Anxiety
Risk for impaired walking

rationale.correct: Use ABC and Maslow: actual airway problems come before pain, mobility and psychosocial needs.

perOption.a: Airway problems threaten oxygenation and come first under ABC priorities.
perOption.b: Pain is important, and managing it helps coughing, but airway clearance is the higher priority.
perOption.c: Psychosocial needs come after physiological ones.
perOption.d: A potential problem ranks below an actual airway problem.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?

options.text: A client with cirrhosis has a distended abdomen with a fluid wave
A client 2 hours after a colonoscopy with polyp removal has a rigid, board-like abdomen
A client with pneumonia is coughing up yellow sputum
A client after total knee replacement rates pain 5 out of 10

rationale.correct: Separate expected findings of a known condition from unexpected findings that suggest a complication.

perOption.a: Ascites is an expected finding in cirrhosis.
perOption.b: A rigid abdomen after colonoscopy suggests bowel perforation and peritonitis.
perOption.c: Purulent sputum is expected with bacterial pneumonia.
perOption.d: Moderate pain is expected after joint replacement.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The nurse has just received report. Place the clients in the order the nurse should see them, from first to last.

items.text: A client with diabetes who is alert, with a glucose of 62 mg/dL
A client 4 hours after a thyroidectomy who has new stridor
A client 2 hours after surgery with a saturated dressing, heart rate 116/min and blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg
A client who needs discharge teaching before going home this afternoon
A client 1 day after surgery requesting pain medication for pain rated 6 out of 10

rationale.correct: Order by airway, breathing and circulation first, then other physiological needs, then teaching for stable clients.

perOption.a: Airway obstruction is the most immediate threat to life.
perOption.b: Bleeding with signs of shock is a circulation threat; it comes after the airway.
perOption.c: Hypoglycemia needs treatment soon, but the client is alert and can take oral carbohydrate.
perOption.d: Pain is important but stable.
perOption.e: Teaching for a stable client can wait until urgent needs are met.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: The nurse is working with assistive personnel (AP). Which tasks can the nurse delegate to the AP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Measuring intake and output for a client with heart failure
Helping a client walk on the second day after surgery
Assessing the skin of a newly admitted client
Collecting a stool specimen for occult blood
Feeding a client who has dysphagia after a recent stroke
Teaching a client how to use an incentive spirometer

rationale.correct: Delegate tasks that are routine, have predictable outcomes and are for stable clients. Assessment, teaching, evaluation and care of unstable clients stay with the nurse.

perOption.a: Measuring and recording I&O is a standard task with a predictable outcome.
perOption.b: Ambulating a stable client is within the AP's role.
perOption.c: Assessment is an RN responsibility and cannot be delegated.
perOption.d: Specimen collection is a routine task with a predictable outcome.
perOption.e: A client with dysphagia has a high aspiration risk and needs a licensed nurse or specially trained staff.
perOption.f: Teaching is an RN responsibility; the AP may remind the client to use it after the RN teaches.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Choose tasks that can be delegated to assistive personnel.

questions.stem: For each task, indicate the staff member the RN should assign it to. Choose the person with the most limited scope who can safely do the task.

rows.text: Admission assessment of a newly admitted client
Giving scheduled oral medications to a stable client
Reinforcing low-sodium diet teaching the RN started
Helping a stable client walk to the bathroom
Giving IV push morphine to a client after surgery
Developing the plan of care for a new client

rationale.correct: RNs keep assessment, planning, initial teaching, evaluation and unstable clients. LPNs care for stable clients, give most medications and reinforce teaching. APs do routine tasks.

perOption.r1:c2: LPNs collect data but can't do the initial assessment.
perOption.r2:c1: The RN could do this, but the LPN can safely do it too.
perOption.r2:c2: Giving medications to stable clients is within LPN scope.
perOption.r2:c3: APs don't give medications in acute care.
perOption.r3:c1: The RN can, but reinforcing existing teaching is within LPN scope.
perOption.r3:c2: LPNs reinforce teaching the RN has done.
perOption.r4:c3: Ambulating a stable client is a routine AP task.
perOption.r5:c1: IV push opioids need RN assessment before and after.
perOption.r5:c2: In most states, LPNs may not give IV push medications.
perOption.r6:c1: Planning care is an RN responsibility.
perOption.r6:c2: LPNs contribute data but don't develop the plan.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: Which client is most appropriate for the RN to assign to an LPN?

options.text: A client with stable type 2 diabetes who needs sliding-scale insulin and a simple dressing change
A client who had a tracheostomy placed 4 hours ago
A client in the first 15 minutes of a blood transfusion
A client who needs an admission assessment

rationale.correct: Assign the LPN stable clients with predictable outcomes whose care uses standard procedures.

perOption.a: This client is stable, and the care involves routine skills within LPN scope.
perOption.b: A new tracheostomy carries a risk of airway complications and needs RN assessment.
perOption.c: The early part of a transfusion is when reactions happen; the RN monitors the client.
perOption.d: Admission assessment is an RN responsibility.

questions.stem: A nurse who usually works in pediatrics is floated to an adult medical-surgical unit. Which client should the charge nurse assign to this nurse?

options.text: A client with pneumonia receiving IV antibiotics
A client with a new chest tube after a thoracotomy
A client on telemetry with a new second-degree heart block
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion

rationale.correct: Float nurses get stable clients whose care doesn't need unit-specific expertise.

perOption.a: This stable client's care uses skills that any RN has, so it's suitable for a floating nurse.
perOption.b: A new chest tube needs experience with adult surgical complications.
perOption.c: An unstable cardiac rhythm needs a nurse experienced in cardiac care.
perOption.d: An insulin infusion with hourly titration is complex and unstable care.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that a client's blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg. Two hours ago it was 132/80 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the AP to recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour
Give the client a PRN antihypertensive right away
Go to the client, recheck the blood pressure and assess the client
Document the reading and tell the next shift

rationale.correct: The RN keeps responsibility for evaluating data that an AP collects; abnormal findings need the nurse's own assessment.

perOption.a: Waiting delays assessment of a significant change.
perOption.b: The nurse must confirm the reading and assess the client first.
perOption.c: An unexpected change reported by an AP needs the nurse's own assessment.
perOption.d: A significant change must be acted on, not handed off.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Follow up on abnormal data reported by assistive personnel.

questions.stem: The nurse is delegating vital sign checks for a client after surgery to assistive personnel. Which instruction is best?

options.text: "Take the vital signs and let me know if anything is abnormal."
"Take the vital signs every hour and tell me right away if the systolic pressure is below 100 or the heart rate is above 110."
"Check the vital signs when you have time."
"Take the vital signs and decide whether the client needs pain medication."

rationale.correct: Effective delegation gives specific instructions: what, when and which findings to report.

perOption.a: The AP may not know which values are abnormal for this client.
perOption.b: Clear frequency and specific values to report meet the right-communication part of delegation.
perOption.c: This gives no frequency or reporting criteria.
perOption.d: Decisions about medication need nursing judgment and can't be delegated.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Give clear, specific instructions when delegating.

questions.stem: The nurse asks assistive personnel to insert a straight urinary catheter. The AP says, "I've never been trained to do that." What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Tell the AP to watch a video and then do the procedure
Ask the AP to do it with another AP watching
Do the catheterization or assign it to competent staff, and arrange training for the AP
Report the AP to the nurse manager for refusing an assignment

rationale.correct: Under the right-person part of delegation, the delegatee must be competent; the nurse stays responsible for the care being done.

perOption.a: A video doesn't confirm competence.
perOption.b: Another AP can't supervise or verify competence.
perOption.c: Only competent staff may do a delegated task; the nurse ensures the care is done and addresses the training gap.
perOption.d: Declining a task outside one's competence is appropriate, not insubordination.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: The nurse calls the provider about a client whose urine output has dropped. Place the nurse's statements in SBAR order.

items.text: "I'm calling about Mr. Lee in room 12, whose urine output has been 15 mL/hr for the last 3 hours."
"He's 2 days after a bowel resection and has been receiving IV fluids at 75 mL/hr."
"I'd like an order for a fluid bolus and a basic metabolic panel. Can you see him within the hour?"
"His blood pressure is 96/60, heart rate 108, and his mucous membranes are dry. I think he may be volume depleted."

rationale.correct: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) organizes urgent communication so key information isn't missed.

perOption.a: Situation: what is happening now.
perOption.b: Background: the relevant history and treatment.
perOption.c: Assessment: the nurse's findings and interpretation.
perOption.d: Recommendation: what the nurse thinks is needed.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: During end-of-shift handoff for a client 1 day after surgery, which information is most important to report?

options.text: The client's family visited in the afternoon
The client's oxygen saturation dropped to 90% at 1500 and the client is now on 2 L/min of oxygen
The client prefers to shower in the evening
The client ate 75% of lunch

rationale.correct: Handoff should highlight changes in condition, new interventions and pending follow-up.

perOption.a: Visits rarely affect the next shift's priorities.
perOption.b: A change in condition and a new intervention need follow-up by the oncoming nurse.
perOption.c: Preferences are useful but not the priority.
perOption.d: Normal intake is useful but less important than a change in respiratory status.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke coughs and chokes when drinking water. Which referral should the nurse request?

options.text: Physical therapist
Speech-language pathologist
Occupational therapist
Respiratory therapist

rationale.correct: Coughing or choking while drinking suggests dysphagia; the speech-language pathologist evaluates swallowing.

perOption.a: PT focuses on mobility, strength and gait.
perOption.b: An SLP assesses swallowing and recommends diet textures and techniques to prevent aspiration.
perOption.c: OT focuses on fine motor skills and activities of daily living.
perOption.d: RT manages breathing treatments and ventilation, not swallowing.

Physical therapist
Dietitian

perOption.b: PT addresses walking, strength and large-muscle function.

questions.stem: Which client findings should prompt the nurse to call the rapid response team? Select all that apply.

options.text: New confusion in a client who was alert and oriented 1 hour ago
Oxygen saturation of 87% despite 4 L/min of oxygen
Heart rate of 136/min
Systolic blood pressure of 84 mm Hg
Chronic back pain rated 6 out of 10
Temperature of 37.9 °C (100.2 °F)

rationale.correct: Rapid response teams are called for acute changes in mental status, breathing, heart rate, blood pressure or oxygenation, before a cardiac arrest happens.

perOption.a: An acute change in mental status is an early warning sign of deterioration.
perOption.b: Persistent hypoxemia despite oxygen meets rapid response criteria.
perOption.c: Heart rates over about 130/min are a common rapid response trigger.
perOption.d: Hypotension under 90 mm Hg signals possible shock.
perOption.e: Chronic pain is managed through the usual plan of care.
perOption.f: A low-grade temperature alone doesn't meet rapid response criteria.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: The nurse reviews morning laboratory results for six clients. Highlight the results that require immediate follow-up.

cells: Client taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation
Client with an upper GI bleed

rationale.correct: Critical values that threaten the heart, oxygen delivery or the brain need immediate follow-up; expected or therapeutic results don't.

perOption.r1: Hyperkalemia above 6 mEq/L can cause life-threatening dysrhythmias.
perOption.r2: An INR of 2 to 3 is therapeutic for atrial fibrillation.
perOption.r3: Hemoglobin below 7 g/dL with active bleeding usually needs a transfusion.
perOption.r4: A mild rise in WBC is common after surgery.
perOption.r5: A glucose under 54 mg/dL is clinically significant hypoglycemia and needs treatment now.
perOption.r6: This sodium level is within the normal range (135 to 145).

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four phone messages. Which call should the nurse return first?

options.text: A client 1 day after discharge from a TURP who has bright red urine with clots and cannot urinate
A client taking an opioid who has not had a bowel movement in 2 days
A client asking whether to take a statin in the morning or the evening
A client 1 week after a knee arthroscopy who rates pain 3 out of 10

rationale.correct: Return calls about possible complications first: urinary retention with active bleeding.

perOption.a: Clots with an inability to void suggest catheter or urethral obstruction with bleeding; retention and hemorrhage need urgent care.
perOption.b: Constipation needs teaching but isn't urgent.
perOption.c: A medication timing question isn't urgent.
perOption.d: Mild pain is expected and stable.

Giving a scheduled intramuscular injection to a stable client
Doing the first teaching for a client starting insulin
Assessing a client who has just come back from surgery
Evaluating a client's response to a new antihypertensive

rationale.correct: LPNs can give most medications to stable clients and reinforce teaching; RNs keep initial assessment, teaching and evaluation.

perOption.a: Reinforcing teaching the RN has done is within LPN scope.
perOption.b: Giving IM medications to stable clients is within LPN scope.
perOption.c: Initial teaching is an RN responsibility.
perOption.d: Initial post-op assessment of a potentially unstable client is an RN responsibility.

questions.stem: Which instruction from the RN to assistive personnel is inappropriate?

options.text: "Please help Mr. Ruiz with his shower this morning."
"Please check Mrs. Chen's IV site and tell me if it looks infected."
"Please record how much Ms. Patel drinks during your shift."
"Please help Mr. Ali turn every 2 hours."

rationale.correct: APs can report what they see, but judging whether a finding is normal is an assessment that stays with the nurse.

perOption.a: Hygiene care for a stable client can be delegated.
perOption.b: Deciding whether an IV site is infected is an assessment; the AP can't make that judgment.
perOption.c: Measuring intake is an appropriate AP task.
perOption.d: Repositioning is an appropriate AP task.

questions.stem: One hour after surgery, a client rates pain 8 out of 10, feels nauseated, is anxious and has an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the prescribed IV opioid
Give the prescribed antiemetic
Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
Stay with the client and offer reassurance

rationale.correct: Treat the oxygenation problem first. Anxiety and restlessness can be early signs of hypoxemia.

perOption.a: Opioids can depress breathing further; oxygenation comes first.
perOption.b: Nausea matters but isn't the most urgent problem.
perOption.c: Hypoxemia is the most immediate threat; positioning and oxygen improve it quickly.
perOption.d: Reassurance helps, but the cause of the anxiety may be hypoxemia.
